discovery: The titanium-sapphire laser and passive mode-locking techniques (Kerr-lens and semiconductor saturable absorber) that made femtosecond solid-state lasers practical

nominees.name: Peter F. Moulton
nominees.affiliation: MIT Lincoln Laboratory (formerly Q-Peak Inc.), USA

motivation: Moulton's invention of the titanium-doped sapphire laser (1982) gave physics a broadly tunable gain medium with bandwidth for pulses of a few optical cycles. Sibbett's discovery of self-mode-locking (1991), explained as Kerr-lens mode-locking, turned it into a simple, robust source of femtosecond pulses. Keller's semiconductor saturable absorber mirror (SESAM, 1992) made passive mode-locking reliable and self-starting across solid-state and later semiconductor and fibre lasers. Together these advances replaced fragile dye lasers and made ultrafast lasers turnkey laboratory tools. They underpin chirped pulse amplification systems, frequency combs, attosecond science, multiphoton microscopy, femtochemistry and ophthalmic and industrial micromachining. Nearly every ultrafast experiment in the world today begins with one of their oscillators. This enabling work opened whole fields of physics, chemistry, biology and medicine, and it has gone unrecognised for more than three decades.
